Grand-place: Here you are, at the historic heart of Mons. Look up: among all these façades, from Gothic to Neoclassical, which one draws your eye first? The 15th-century Town Hall dominates the square. On the ground, a 12-metre ring of blue stone marks the spot of the Lumeçon, the combat of Saint George and the Dragon.
Fontaine du Rouge Puits: This fountain of 1833 is the work of Albert Jamot. It was once painted entirely red — hence its name. Look up: what do you see at the very top of the column? And around the basin, how many faces are spouting water?
Immeuble Blanc Lévrier: This town house of 1530 is one of the finest on the Grand-Place. Scan the blue-stone façade: can you find the two greyhounds and the inscription « AV BLAN LEVRIE »? Higher up, a coat of arms evokes Charles V and the Golden Fleece.
Immeuble Grand Place 31 34: Around 1709, four houses were designed as a single block. The façades seem to run on without a break. In your view, how many bays do you count along the Grand-Place, from left to right? The stone bands tie sills and lintels from one end to the other.
Office du Tourisme: You are standing in front of an 18th-century Classical building, renovated in 2013 to house the Tourist Office. Compare the façade with its neighbours: what was carefully preserved, despite the modernisation of the interior?
Hotel de la Couronne: Between 1766 and 1772, Fonson raised this Louis XV town house in place of the « Grise Ostriche ». Look at the balconies, the pilasters, the curved pediments. Do you find the façade perfectly symmetrical… or does something feel off?
Chapelle Saint Georges: This Renaissance chapel of 1601, tucked against the Town Hall, was the aldermen’s oratory. Look for the entrance — it is discreet. Imagine a rood screen, gone around 1880, that let the magistrate attend the service without leaving the salon des États. Can you still see it in the volume of the building?
Immeuble Grand Place 28 30: Three houses in blue stone, a single 18th-century ensemble. Let your eye travel from left to right: which one stands out with a wrought-iron balcony? That is number 29. A single roof now covers the whole.
Immeuble Grand Place 14: At the corner of rue du Miroir, this 18th-century building turns its back to the square and its profile to the street. Walk around the corner: does the side façade have the same rhythm as the one on the Grand-Place? Below, as so often here, a shop occupies the ground floor.
Theatre Royal: Inaugurated in 1843, the Théâtre Royal nearly vanished in a fire in 1869. Step up to the railings: do you know the figures represented there? The Neoclassical façade, with its columns, was meant to rival Belgium’s great stages.
Singe du Grand Garde: The most famous Mons native is tiny, and fixed to the façade. Can you see him, crouching, scratching his cheek? His polished skull is no accident: thousands of hands have stroked it for luck. Try it, with the left hand, if you like.
Statue du Dragon: To the right of the Town Hall steps, two bronzes by Gérard Garouste, inaugurated in 2006. Saint George wears a helmet. As for the dragon… how do you find him? Fierce, ironic, almost familiar? It is already the combat of the Ducasse, frozen in metal.
Hotel de Ville: Look at the façade of the Town Hall. What surprises you? Begun in 1458 by Mathieu de Layens, it has only two storeys: a planned floor was never built. Right at the top, the Renaissance campanile houses the Bancloque, a bell of 1390.
Ropieur: This bronze street urchin, inaugurated in 1937, is the work of Léon Gobert. Step closer: where does the jet of water come from, and what exactly is the Ropieur doing? They say he sprays passers-by. Look also, under his heel, for the sculptor’s initials.
Gillis: Marcel Gillis (1897-1972) was a painter, caricaturist, poet and singer. In front of his bust or his plaque, what stays with you of an artist with so many faces? He was also curator of the Museum of Fine Arts for nearly forty years.
Mayeur: You are entering a hidden garden behind the Town Hall, laid out in the 1930s. Look up at the century-old trees: beech, limes, a horse chestnut… Which ones do you recognise? Along the way, the Ropieur is never far.
Musee du Doudou: Here, in the former Mont-de-Piété, the Ducasse is told — UNESCO heritage. Before you go in, a question for the eye: do you already know what the Lumeçon is, that combat of Saint George and the Dragon? The museum shows it to you, gesture by gesture.
Conservatoire Royal: Since 1873, music has lived in a former convent, rue de Nimy. As you pass, listen: do you hear a piano, a voice, a bow? The Conservatory, founded in 1820, is today part of ARTS².
Eglise Sainte Elisabeth: Look up at the bell tower. This church, consecrated in 1588, burned in 1714 and was then raised again. On the façade, what remains of the Gothic, and what gives away the Baroque restoration? Elisabeth of Hungary is its patron saint.
Palais de Justice: This Neoclassical façade in Soignies stone dates from the 1840s. Count the columns, the pediment, the staircase: what does it make you think of, a temple or a palace? Since 1975, the Court of Appeal of Mons has sat here.
Maison Losseau: The façade looks well-behaved, almost too well-behaved. Would you guess that inside lies one of the finest Art Nouveau interiors in Belgium? From 1899, Léon Losseau brought in electricity and central heating — a first in Mons.
Maison Rue de Nimy 53: A listed Tournai-style house, today the seat of IDEA. Look at the bands, the projecting sills, the brick and the stone. What, in your view, ties it to the style of Tournai rather than that of the Grand-Place?
Mundaneum: It is called the « paper Google ». Paul Otlet and Henri La Fontaine wanted to classify all the world’s knowledge. In front of the building, imagine millions of index cards: where would you begin? La Fontaine received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1913.
Place du Parc: Stop in the middle of the square. Its shape is neither a square nor a circle: can you see the lozenge? It was once called place Saint-Jean. A bandstand and a statue of Roland de Lassus disappeared here, victims of the Great War.
Chapelle des Visitandines: This Baroque chapel of 1717, by Bettignies, has lived many lives: convent, prison, archives. Look at the bell tower and the portal. Nothing in this elegance hints that State files were stored here until 2006?
Ancienne Caserne de Gendarmerie: Rue du Rossignol, a barracks of 1870 in red brick and white stone. The style is Flemish Neo-Renaissance. Look for the colour contrasts, the gables, the window bays: does it remind you more of a Flemish town hall… or a barracks?
Prison de Mons: This star-shaped architecture, known as « Ducpétiaux », dates from the 1860s. From the outside, can you guess the wings radiating from the centre? Paul Verlaine was locked up here after shooting Rimbaud. He wrote poems here.
Tour Valenciennoise: You are facing the last tower of the medieval enclosure. Step up to the facing: these walls are up to four metres thick. Can you feel their mass? Raised in 1358, it survived the demolition of the ramparts in 1818.
Pavillons Caserne Cavalerie: These pavilions recall the Léopold barracks, built around 1840 for men and horses. Look for the former stables in the rhythm of the bays. How many soldiers do you imagine here, in the days of the 2nd Regiment of Chasseurs à cheval?
Tank Sherman: In front of the Mons Memorial Museum, a Sherman M4A1 named « In the Mood ». Walk around it: do you see the traces of a fighting machine, or rather of a monument? It commemorates the liberation of Mons, in September 1944.
Machine a Eau: This engineer’s building, 1869-1871, pumped water from Spiennes thanks to the Trouille. Look for the wheel, the basins, the industrial brick. In your view, why did Mons invest so much in drinking water in the 19th century?
Parc du Waux Hall: Five hectares of public garden, laid out by Louis Fuchs in the 1860s. At the centre, an eclectic pavilion. Which path do you take first? The one that leads to the bandstand, to the trees, or to the building? The City bought the park in 1892.
Eglise Saint Nicolas: First parish outside the walls, from 1224. A fire in 1664 left only the tower. Compare the bell tower and the rest of the church: do you see two periods stuck together? The Baroque reconstruction ran until 1702.
Chapelle du Belian: A small chapel of 1775, urban refuge of the canonesses of Bélian. Its Classical façade is almost too discreet. What, for you, still says « chapel » rather than « private house »? UMONS sometimes presents exhibitions here.
Marche aux Herbes: It is often called the Petit Marché. From 1409, goods were sold here differently than on the Grand-Place. Imagine the Fontaine du Rouge-Puits here, until 1955. In your view, why was it moved away first… then brought back to the Grand-Place?
Maison Rue de la Couronne 20 22: An 18th-century house, four bays, three storeys. The street links the Grand-Place to Nimy. Turning around, do you still see the square, or already another district? Count the bays: is the rhythm regular?
Couvent des Soeurs Noires: Their name comes from the black scapular. Settled here in 1498, they cared for the sick, especially during the plagues. In front of the convent, what remains of a place of charity? Look for the chapel, the porch, the wall that once closed the city.
Carre des Arts: This was the Caserne Guillaume, 1824, for the chasseurs à pied. Today it is an art school, ARTS². Does the military Neoclassical façade still look like a barracks, or already like a campus? Rémi de Puydt drew its lines.
Anciens Abattoirs: Charles Sury built these halls in 1854. Closed in 1984, they now house contemporary art. Look up at the glass roofs and the timber frames: can you still guess the original function, or only an exhibition space?
Eglise Notre Dame de Messines: Rue de Bertaimont, this church was first called Saint-Nicolas en Bertaimont. A painting of the Virgin, found in the cemetery, made it a place of pilgrimage. On the portal or the bell tower, do you see traces of that Marian devotion?
Maison Rue de Bertaimont 17: An 18th-century Mons house, listed in 1988. We are in Messines, the district of the giants since 1620. The blue stone, the window bays, the bands: what, here, says « Mons » to you rather than another Walloon town?
Maison Rue de Bertaimont 33: Three storeys, three bays. Look at the right-hand bay: wider, set back, with a door and a balcony. Why this offset, in your view? A nobler entrance, a former shop, an addition? The district lived through the siege of 1691.
Casemates: Twelve vaults, built under the Kingdom of the Netherlands for 2,000 soldiers… who never came. Line yourself up facing the arcades: can you count them in a single glance? The façade stretches over more than 160 metres.
Bonne Maison de Bouzanton: In 1562, Louise de Bouzanton founded an orphanage here for poor children. The Hôtel de Bavière no longer looks like an asylum. What, in the façade, still gives away an institution rather than a town house?
Chapelle du Beguinage: Founded in 1248 by Margaret of Constantinople, this chapel is the remnant of the beguinage of Cantimpret. The Hainaut Gothic style dates from 1549. Look for traces of an enclosure of pious women: a portal, a wall, a vanished garden?
Tour du Val des Ecoliers: Only a tower remains. The abbey of Val des Écoliers, founded in 1252, was demolished in 1876. Walk around it: imagine the church, the cloister, the buildings. What is missing most, in your view, to still make it an « abbey »?
Gare de Mons: The first station dated from 1841. This one, Calatrava’s white bridge, changed everything. Look up under the sail of concrete and steel: does it make you think of a bird, a boat, a spine? Behind it, the historic city begins again.
Statue Saint Georges: Place des Congrès, 2024, a bronze by Xavier Veilhan. Saint George and the dragon, contemporary version. The style is pared down, almost abstract. Do you still recognise the warrior saint… or do you mainly see a silhouette of public art?
Lucie et les Papillons: More than seven metres of steel: a little girl, broken scissors, butterflies. From which side does the work speak to you first? Childhood, love, fragility? David Mesguich drew on his daughter Lucie, and on « butterflies in the stomach ».
Collegiale Sainte Waudru: A masterpiece of Brabantine Gothic, begun in 1450, 115 metres long. Step back to see the whole. The tower, though, stops short: did you know 190 metres were planned? Work stopped in 1691, at roof height.
Tresors de Sainte Waudru: Here a ring is kept, and the clasp known as the « Benoîte Affique », from the 7th century. If you visit the Treasury, look for these tiny objects: how can a whole city fit inside a clasp? The shrouds cover the bones of the saint foundress.
Le Car d Or: This Louis XVI chariot, 1779-1782, comes out once a year for the Ducasse. Look at the sculptures, the gilding, the shrine. In your view, how many people does it take to haul it up the ramp, on Trinity Sunday? The procession of the relics goes back to the plague of 1349.
Porte Rue Courte: A Gothic doorway reused in an 18th-century house. It comes from the abbey of Val des Écoliers. Look up at the lintel: do you see the ogee arch, the finials, the crockets of Flamboyant Gothic?
Maison Espagnole: After the fire of 1548, they rebuilt in red brick, stepped gables, mullioned windows. This is called Scheldt architecture. Count the « pas de moineau » of the gable: how many steps up to the ridge?
Chapelle Saint Calixte: 1051: Richilde has this chapel built for the relics of Pope Callixtus. It is the oldest religious building in Mons, in Bray sandstone. Touch the stone with your eyes: do you find it rougher, older than the collegiate church nearby?
Ancien Chateau Comtal: Baldwin IV, the Builder, placed here the fortress of the counts of Hainaut. Only fragments remain. Can you link, with your eye, the enclosure, the Tour César and Saint-Calixte? It was both a residence and a centre of power.
Tour Cesar: In the park of the Château, this tower base is a remnant of the comital castle. It is no longer a complete tower. How high do you imagine it rose, in the 13th or 14th century? The 19th-century garden has absorbed it.
Beffroi: El Catiau, 87 metres, Belgium’s only Baroque belfry. Look up to the top. In your view, how many bells are there up there? The carillon plays every quarter of an hour: « El Grosse Cloche du Catiau », « La Bière », « Zandrine »…
Square: This garden of 1887 covers the former Saint-Germain Collegiate Church, destroyed at the Revolution. Under your feet, a church has vanished. The fountain honours the volunteers of 1830. Can you still see, in the layout of the paths, the plan of a choir?
Pilori: A triangular fountain of 1779, Écaussinnes blue stone, at the foot of Sainte-Waudru. It was not mere decoration: water really flowed here. Look for the vase, the pyramid, the arms of the chapter. Do you still find a fountain… or already a monument?
